title: Glaw Lake and Elephant Corridor Orders

text:
Glaw Lake in Arunachal Pradesh was designated a Ramsar site on 3 August 2026, Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav announced. The freshwater lake becomes India's 101st Ramsar site and the first wetland of international importance in Arunachal Pradesh. Yadav said India's Ramsar network had grown from 26 sites in 2014 to 101 sites, describing the designation as a milestone for the state and for wetland conservation across the country.

The lake lies within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve and Kamlang Wildlife Sanctuary in Lohit district, in the Eastern Himalayas. It is fed by perennial mountain streams and surrounded by dense forest. The Ministry said the designation would support biodiversity protection, climate resilience, water conservation and the livelihoods of communities dependent on the wetland. A site-specific restoration plan is being prepared, with the active participation of the Mishmi community.

Elephant corridors also drew attention this month. On 17 August 2026, the Supreme Court directed the Union Environment Ministry to conduct a fresh nationwide survey of elephant corridors and to report on the obstructions within them. A bench said corridors had been impeded, blocked or obstructed despite existing ministry guidelines, and that crop damage could not justify barriers. The court also prohibited the use of fireballs and mashaals, or torches, to drive elephants away from human-dominated areas, and directed state authorities to enforce its directions. The bench said states could not block elephant movement routes.

In late August 2026, Tamil Nadu notified three elephant corridors within the Cauvery North Wildlife Sanctuary in the Hosur forest division. The notification followed interim directions from the Madras High Court and recommendations of committees set up to identify corridors and bottlenecks. The three corridors cover more than 10,300 hectares. They include the Jawalagiri-Ulibanda-Thaggatti corridor, about 18.5 km long, and the Bilikkal-Jawalagiri corridor, about 2.2 km long. The Chief Wildlife Warden said all three lie within reserved forest and sanctuary land, and that no private land or revenue village is affected.

The corridors sit on the trans-Cauvery route used by elephants moving between Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. Officials said the notification is meant to protect traditional migration routes, especially during seasonal monsoon movements.
